# Risk-sharing partnership (commenda, mudaraba) (`partnership_commenda`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/economy.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Economy & finance (`economy`)
- Deps: helped by double_entry, alphabet_writing
- Core idea: An investor puts up the capital, a travelling merchant puts in his work; profit is split in an agreed share (in Genoa commonly three quarters to the investor, one quarter to the traveller), while losses fall on the capital, so the traveller risks only his labour. Savers who cannot travel can finance voyages, a merchant without money can trade, and an investor can spread his wealth over many small ventures. Because it shares profit rather than charging interest, it fitted both Islamic and Christian usury rules. The agent must keep accounts and return to settle; a written contract registered with a notary or witnesses fixes shares, route and duration.
- Pitfalls:
  - Treating it as a loan with interest: if the voyage fails, the investor gets nothing back
  - Forgetting the agent problem: a distant partner can hide profits, so accounts, reputation and merchant courts are needed
  - Confusing it with a general partnership, where every partner is liable with all his property for the firm's debts
  - Expecting it to fund a long-lived enterprise: each commenda ends with one voyage or term, which is why joint-stock companies were later needed
- History: mesopotamia: c. 1900 BC – Old Assyrian naruqqum ('bag'): a dozen or so investors pool gold for a Kanesh merchant for about ten years, sharing profit; islamic: 8th c. – mudaraba (qirad) set out in Hanafi law (al-Shaybani), widely used in Mediterranean and Indian Ocean trade; europe: 10th–12th c. – Venetian colleganza and Genoese commenda, recorded in notarial registers from the 1150s; 1408 Florence allows the accomandita, a limited partnership with a passive partner liable only for his stake; china: Ming–Qing – hehuo partnerships pool capital from several investors for a managing partner
- Read:
  - Abraham L. Udovitch, Partnership and Profit in Medieval Islam (1970)
  - Robert S. Lopez & Irving W. Raymond, Medieval Trade in the Mediterranean World (1955)
  - Mogens Trolle Larsen, Ancient Kanesh: A Merchant Colony in Bronze Age Anatolia (2015)
